analysis.one_liner: Bars states from punishing people who travel out of state for legal abortion care.
analysis.headline: The bill had 41 Senate sponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, but was referred to the Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor time before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for any state or person to punish, discriminate against, or interfere with someone who travels to another state to get or provide reproductive health care that is legal where it is given — including abortion — or who helps them travel. It would let the Justice Department and affected patients, helpers, and clinics sue to enforce that right, would override conflicting state laws, and would strip state governments of immunity in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and others who live in states that ban or restrict abortion and need to cross state lines for care, along with the friends, employers, and organizations that help them travel and the clinics that treat them. The bill would shield all of them from lawsuits, penalties, or retaliation, and would give them (and the Justice Department) the power to sue states that try to interfere.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women in states with abortion bans

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any person or government to restrict, sanction, discriminate against, or otherwise disadvantage anyone who travels to another state for reproductive health care that is legal in that state, or who helps someone make that trip.

Protects out-of-state patients from being denied rights or benefits, and protects clinics from punishment for treating patients who live in ban states, as long as the same care would be legal for a local patient.

Gives the Attorney General a way to sue states that interfere, and gives patients, helpers, and clinics their own right to sue in state or federal court, with damages, injunctions, and attorney's fees available to winners.

Overrides any conflicting state law and explicitly waives state sovereign immunity, qualified immunity, and Eleventh Amendment immunity, so states and officials could actually be hauled into court rather than hiding behind immunity doctrines.

analysis.who_pays: State governments with abortion bans and other restrictions, which would lose the ability to enforce penalties against residents who travel for care, the people who help them, and clinics that treat out-of-state patients. Their laws could be struck down in court, with attorney's fees going to plaintiffs who win. There is no significant fiscal cost to ordinary taxpayers beyond Justice Department enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The bill offers legal protection but no money: it does nothing to pay for travel, lodging, child care, or the care itself, so cost remains the biggest barrier for low-income women in ban states even if the law worked as written.

The bill bans interference by 'any person,' not just governments, but recent Supreme Court precedent (including the Dobbs decision the bill cites) limits Congress's power to regulate purely private conduct under the Fourteenth Amendment, so courts could narrow or strike parts of it.

Preempting state laws and waiving state immunity is a significant shift of power from states to federal courts, which critics would call an overreach into areas states have traditionally regulated; supporters would answer that the right to travel is itself a constitutional right.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a woman in a state that bans abortion, the bill's protections are real and potentially valuable: no lawsuit, penalty, or retaliation for crossing a state line, backed by a private right to sue. The weaknesses are that it covers only the legal interference, not the money burden, and that parts of it rest on legal theories a hostile Supreme Court could trim back. It is a strong, if incomplete, protection whose main failure was that it never moved at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on June 20, 2023 with 36 original cosponsors and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill attracted 40 cosponsors in total — 39 Democrats and 1 independent — but no Republican signed on.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action: there is no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action in the record, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments with abortion bans keep their authority to restrict, penalize, or deter residents from traveling for care, since the bill never became law. Women in those states gained nothing, and the clinics serving them remain exposed to legal pressure.

for.name: Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 20, 2023 and recruited 36 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 40 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 39 Democrats and 1 independent, including Senators Durbin, Murray, Warren, Sanders, and Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the entire Democratic caucus plus one independent but no Republican support.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the Senate's 49 Republicans cosponsored the bill, leaving it far short of the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster and reach a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors were Democrats or allied independents and no Republican cosponsored; because the bill never got a vote, sponsorship is the only measure of the split.

industries.note: The bill would shield clinics from punishment for treating out-of-state patients and would let providers sue on behalf of themselves, their staff, and their patients, with attorney's fees paid by losing states. For patients in ban states, that protection keeps clinics open as the only path to legal care.

industries.industry: Employers and nonprofits helping workers or clients travel for care
industries.note: The bill would make it unlawful to sanction or discriminate against anyone who assists with travel for legal out-of-state care, protecting companies and charities that cover or arrange such travel from state retaliation.
